scene: Child: (head down on the table, not looking at the tablet)
Parent: Mom.
Child: (head still down, not looking at the tablet)
Parent: I'm just waiting.
Child: (raises head and looks at the tablet)
Parent: Read.
Child: (staring at the tablet)
Parent: No, we have to wait for them to send it and then we start.
Child: (hands on cheeks, looks at the tablet attentively)
Parent: Okay.
Child: (focused on the tablet, pointing at it)
Parent: Mm-hmm (affirmative). At...
Child: (continues looking and interacting with the tablet)
Parent: Mm-hmm (affirmative)
Child: (still engaged, pointing at the screen)
Parent: ...The...
(child and parent continue to interact with the tablet)
Parent: Mm-hmm (affirmative)
Child: (continues reading or interacting with the tablet)
Parent: ...Oath...
Child: (engaged, hand on chin)
Parent: Yup.
Child: (looks interested, still at the tablet)
Parent: (a person in blue shirt comes over)
Child: (still focused on the tablet)
Person in Blue Shirt: (interacts with the headgear of the parent, possibly adjusting it)
Child: (continues interacting with the tablet)
Parent: (waiting while the headgear is adjusted)
Child: Can I?
Person in Blue Shirt: Sure.
Child: (still focused on the tablet)
Person in Blue Shirt: (interacts with the tablet, possibly helping the child) There you go.
Child: (Looking at the tablet with a neutral expression)
Parent: "You look so ugly. You look [inaudible 00:00:50] Warm and white."
Child: (Remains looking at the tablet)
Parent: "All right, so, here you can just click here for next page, click here for the previous page..."
Child: "Okay"
Parent: "... and also go back to bookshelf if you don't like it."
Child: "Okay"
Parent: "And also, here is the starting point"
Child: "Okay"
Child: (Reaches out to the tablet)
Child: "Okay, I want to push it."
Parent: "Wait. We weren't- see, okay!"
Child: (Interacts with the tablet)
Child: (touching the tablet screen)
Parent: I actually know that one.
Child: (pointing at the screen)
Parent: You want Lorax, you said.
Child: No want...
Parent: You changed your mind?
Child: (looking at the screen thoughtfully)
Parent: And also one short thing, you can just do your action readings at home.
Child: (sitting back and looking at the tablet)
Parent: Okay.
Child: (reaching towards the tablet and then sitting back with hands on the table)
Parent: So, if you're [crosstalk 00:01:33]
Child: (looking attentively at the tablet)
Parent: Okay. We want this one? We read this one.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "No, but I really like..."
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Ugh! All right. Ready? What was it called again?"
Child: (smiling)
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "Cloudy."
Child: (nodding)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Okay. All right."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Yes, [inaudible]"
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Hit first page. Okay, so this was Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs, right?"
Child: "Yeah!"
Child: (smiling and shifting in chair)
Parent: "Okay! All right. Ready?"
Child: "Yeah."
Child: (leaning closer to the tablet)

Parent: "We were all sitting around the big kitchen table. It was Saturday morning. Just like this, Saturday morning. Pancake morning, mom was squeezing oranges for juice. Henry and I were betting on how many pancakes we could each eat. And Grandpa was doing the flipping."
Child: (listening attentively)
Child: (interacts with the tablet, possibly swiping the screen)
Parent: Do you want to change the page? I think you have to go a little further down. There you go.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: Seconds later, something flew through the air, headed towards the kitchen ceiling, and landed right on Henry.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: What is it?
Child: Pancake.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: Look at the dog and cat too.
Child: (looks up briefly at the parent, then back at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: After we realized that the flying object was only a pancake, we all laughed, even Grandpa. Breakfast continued quite uneventfully. All the other pancake landed in the pan and all of them were eaten, even the one that landed on Henry.
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: That night, touched off by the pancake incident at the breakfast, Grandpa told us the best tall-tale bedtime story he ever told. “Across an ocean, over lots of bumpy mountains, and across three hot deserts and one smaller ocean, there lay the tiny town of Chewandswallow. In most ways, it was very much like any other town. It had a Main Street lined with stores, houses with trees and gardens around them, a schoolhouse, about three hundred people, and some assorted cats and dogs. But there were no food stores in the town of Chewandswallow. They didn't need any. The sky supplied all the food they ever could possibly want. The only thing that was really different about Chewandswallow was its weather. It came three times a day, at breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Everything that everyone ate came from the sky. Whatever the weather served, that was what they ate. But it never rained rain, it never snowed snow, it never just blew wind. It rained things like soup and juice, it snowed mashed potatoes and green peas,” ew, “and sometimes the wind blew in storms of hamburgers.”
Child: (looking at the tablet, smiling, and pointing)
Parent: "Okay, I don't think peas and mashed potatoes would be good. What do you think?"
Child: (interested and attentive, continuing to point and read from the tablet)
Child: (engaged, looking at the tablet while reading)
Parent: (listens attentively, head slightly tilted)

Child: "Well, “The people could watch the weather report on television in the morning, and they would hear the predictions for the next day's food. When the townspeople went outside, they carried their plates, cups, glasses, forks, spoons, knives and napkins with them. That way they would always be prepared for any kind of weather. If there were leftovers, and there usually were, the people took them home, put them in their refrigerator, in case they got hungry in between meals. The menu varied. By the time they woke up in the morning, breakfast was coming down. After a brief shower of orange juice, low clouds of sunny-side-up eggs moved in, followed by pieces of toast. Butter and jellies sprinkled down for the toast. And most of the time, it sprinkled milk afterwards.”"
Child: (still focused on the tablet, brows slightly furrowed)
Parent: (leans closer, resting head on hand)
Child: "It looks very messy, doesn't it? What do they do with all that food?"
Child: (tries to navigate the tablet, looking puzzled)
Parent: (reaches out to assist with tablet navigation)
Child: "I missed, all right, there, Oh no, we went too far. Okay hold on, I have to go back. Where were we? Let's see, which page should we do? We did this one, and this one, Okay. Where did it go?"
Child: (leans in, resting face in hands, reading)
Parent: (leans in closer, following along)

Child: "“For lunch one day, frankfurters, already in the rolls, blew in from the northwest, at about five miles per hour. There were mustard clouds nearby, and then the wind shifted to the east and brought baked beans. Drizzle of soda finished off the meal. Dinner one night consisted of lamb-chops, becoming heavy at times, with occasional ketchup. Periods of peas and baked potatoes were followed by gradual clearing, with a wonderful Jell-O setting in the west.”"
Child: (looking at the tablet, smiling)
Parent: (observes the tablet, leaning on hand)
Child: "Look at that."
Child: (begins speaking, both looking at tablet, slight smile)
Parent: (continues observing, engaged, head resting on hand)
Child: "It’s just like a [crosstalk 00:05:42]"
Child: (reading from the tablet)
Parent: (listening attentively)

Child: "“The Sanitation Department of Chewandswallow had a rather unusual job for a sanitation department. It had to remove the food that fell on the houses and sidewalks and lawns. The workers cleared up things after every meal and fed all the dogs and cats. Then they emptied some of it into the surrounding ocean for the...”
Child: (thinks for a moment, then answers)
Parent: (encourages, smiling)
Child: Fish
Parent: "You think so? "...for the fish and turtles and whales to eat.""
Child: (shrugs slightly, then smiles) "I don't know if that's a good idea. Why don't they compost?"
Child: (looks at tablet, parent reaches to navigate back)
Parent: "The rest, oh wait, go back. Thank you."
Child: (seated and looking at the tablet with a smile)
Parent: (leans in, smiling, indicating)
Child: "The rest of the food was put back into the earth so that the soil would be richer for the people's flower gardens."
Both: (laugh lightly)
Child: (pointing at the tablet while listening)
Parent: "They do compost. Good job."
Child: (smiling and pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "Life for the townspeople was delicious until the weather took a turn for the worse."
Child: (looking intently at the screen)
Parent: "It says, 'Spaghetti ties up town.'"
Child: (leaning forward and pointing at the screen)
Parent: "What is that?"
Child: (still looking at the screen, possibly puzzled)
Parent: "I don't know. Looks like it’s very soggy, don’t they? And then it looks like they’re getting something smelly, and I don’t know, they’re being buried in something over there."
Child: (pointing at the screen)
Parent: "And she's having something but [inaudible 00:06:47]."
Child: (still pointing at the screen)
Parent: "Yeah."
Child: (leaning on hand, looking at the screen)

Parent: "'One day there was nothing by Gorgonzola cheese all day. The next day there was only broccoli, and all overcooked. And the next day there were brussel sprouts and peanut butter with mayonnaise. Another day there was a pea soup fog. No one could see where they were going and they could barely find the rest of the meal. They got stuck in the fog.'"
Child: (leaning on hand, looking at the screen)
Parent: "The food was getting larger and larger and so were the portions. The people were getting frightened. Violent storms blew up frequently. Awful things were happening."
Child: (leaning on hand, looking at the screen)

Parent: "One Tuesday, there was a hurricane of bread and rolls all day long and into the night. There were soft rolls and hard rolls, and some with seeds and some without. There was white bread and rye and whole wheat toast. Most of it was larger than they had ever seen breads and rolls before. It was a terrible day. Everyone had to stay indoors. Roofs were damaged and the Sanitation Department was beside itself. The mess took the workers four days to clean up, and the sea was full of floating rolls."
Child: (pointing at the screen)
Parent: "To help out, the people piled up as much bread as they could into their backyards. The birds picked at it a bit, but it just stayed there, and got staler and staler."
Child: (leaning on hand, looking at the screen)

Parent: "There was a storm of pancakes one morning and a downpour of maple syrup that nearly flooded the town. A huge pancake covered the school. No one could get it off because of its weight, so they had to close the school. Lunch one day brought fifteen-inch drifts of cream cheese and jelly sandwiches. Everyone ate themselves sick and the day ended with a stomachache."
Child: (engaged, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Mm-hmm (affirmative)"
Child: (still engaged, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Do you want to get a new book?"
Child: "Ummm." (slightly pondering, still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "We could also do a shorter book too, if you want."
Child: (excited, pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "Oh my goodness really? It is a Christmas story. Really? Okay!"
Child: (smiling, still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "I like the Grinch."
Child: (focused, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "I need my coffee."
Child: (engaged in reading, turning a page on the tablet)
Parent: "Every Who down in Who-ville liked Christmas a lot. But the Grinch who lived up north of Who-ville did,"
Child: (looks puzzled, turns to the parent)
Parent: "No-no, what did it say?"
Child: (reading again on the tablet)

Parent: "Did not. The Grinch hated Christmas. The whole Christmas season. Now, please don't ask why. No one quite knows the reason. It could be his head wasn't screwed up on just right. It could be perhaps that his shoes were too tight. But I think the most likely reason of all that may have been that his heart was two sizes too small. But whatever the reason is, his heart or his shoes, he stood there on Christmas Eve hating the Whos. Staring down from his cave with a sour Grinchy frown, at the warm lighted windows below in their town. For knew every Who down in Who-ville beneath was busy now, hanging a mistletoe wreath. "And they're hanging their stockings!" he snarled with a sneer. "Tomorrow is Christmas! It iss practically here!" Then he growled with his Grinch fingers nervously drumming "I must find someway to stop Christmas from coming." For he knew tomorrow, he knew."
Child: "What will happen tomorrow?" (curious, looking back at the parent)
Parent: (hugs the child)
Child: (smiling, looking at the tablet again)
Child: (sitting on the parent's lap, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "All the Who girls and boys would wake bright and early. They'd rush for their toys. And then, oh the noise! Oh the noise, noise, noise, noise. The one thing he hated. The NOISE! NOISE! NOISE! NOISE!"
Child: (still sitting on the parent's lap, putting her hands on the table)
Parent: "He does not like noise."
Child: (pointing to the tablet)
Parent: "The noise noise noise noise noise noise NOISE NOISE!"
Child: (leaning on the parent, head resting on parent's shoulder)
Parent: "Right. Okay. Next page."
Child: (moving on parent's lap, adjusting herself)
Parent: "Then the Who."
Child: (still adjusting, moving her body to get comfortable)
Parent: "Okay, what is this? You're arranging yourself. Okay. How are you going to sit? Okay! Okay!"
Child: (leans on the parent again)

Parent: "And then the Whos, young and old, would sit down to a feast. And they'd feast. And they'd feast. And they'd FEAST! FEAST! FEAST! FEAST! They would feast on Who-pudding, a rare Who-roast-beast, which was something the Grinch couldn't stand in the least."
Child: (reaching to touch the tablet)
Parent: "Go ahead."
Child: (putting her hand on the tablet, looking attentive)
Parent: "And, do you know this word? T-H-E-N"
Child: "Then"
Parent: "Then"
Child: (still looking at the tablet, slightly moving)

Parent: "They'd do something he liked the least of all. Every who down in Who-Ville, the tall and the small, would stand close together, with Christmas bells ringing. They'd stand hand in hand and the Whos would start?"
Child: (looking attentive, focuses on the tablet)
Parent: "Singing."
Child: (pointing and looking at the tablet)
Parent: "They'd sing and they'd sing and they'd sing! SING! SING! SING!"
Child: (leaning back slightly, still focused)

Parent: "And the more the Grinch thought of this Who-Christmas song, the more the Grinch thought, “I must stop this whole thing. Why, for fifty-three years I've put up with it now. I must stop Christmas from coming.”"
Child: (looking at the tablet, reaches out to touch it again)
Parent: "But, how?"
Child: (pointing at tablet screen)

Parent: "And then he got an idea. An awful idea. The Grinch got a wonderful, awful idea. “I know just what to do!” The Grinch laughed in his throat. And he made a quick Santy hat and coat. He chuckled and cackled, “What a great Grinchy trick! With this coat and this hat, I look just like Saint Nick!”"
Child: (pointing at the tablet, focused on the story)
Parent: "Ho! Ho! Ho!"
Child: (reaching forward to touch the tablet)

Parent: "I need a reindeer", the grinch looked around. But since reindeer are scarce, there was none to be found. Did that stop old Grinch? No, the Grinch simply said, "If I can't find a reindeer, I'll make one instead." So he called his dog Max, then he took some red thread, and tied a big horn on the top of his head."
Child: (pulling back slightly, still engaged)
Parent: (adjusting the child's position) "Here, oops. Wait a second, [inaudible 00:14:57] up there. Okay. Go ahead!"
Child: (beginning to fidget)
Parent: "And then he loaded some bags and some old empty sacks, on a ramshackle sleigh, and he hitched up old Max."
Child: (starting to wiggly)
Parent: "There. Now you're not such a wiggly squiggly. Okay. Now push."
Child: (calming down, holding the parent)
Parent: "Then Grinch said, "Giddy Up!" And the sleigh started down toward the homes where the Whos lay a-snooze in their town."
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: Next one.
Child: (pointing at an object on the tablet screen)
Parent: That's there.
Child: (looking intently at the screen, hands on the table)
Parent: All their windows were dark. Quiet snow filled the air. All the Who's were dreaming sweet dreams without care. When he came to the first little house on the square,
"This is stop number one," the old Grinchy Claus hissed. And then he climbed to the roof, empty bag in his fist.
Child: (leaning on the parent, looking sad)
Parent: That is so sad.
Child: (pointing to the screen)
Parent: What are all the kids going to do? [crosstalk 00:15:51]
Child: (seems engaged, finger on the screen)

Parent: Then he slid down the chimney, a rather tight pinch, but if Santa could do it, then so could the Grinch. He got stuck only once, for a moment or two, then he stuck his head out of the fireplace flue. Where the little Who stockings hung in a row, "These stockings," he grinned, are the first things to go.
Child: (looking into the tablet, listening)

Parent: He's going to [inaudible 00:16:18] Christmas. Then he slithered and slunk, with a smile most unpleasant, around the whole room, and he took every present. Pop guns, and bicycles, and roller skates, and drums, and checkerboards, and tricycles, and popcorn, and plums, and he stuffed them in bags, then the Grinch very nimbly, stuffed all the bags, one by one, up the chimbley. Then he stunk to the icebox. He took the Whos feast. He took the Who-pudding. He took the roast beast. He cleaned out that icebox as quick as a flash. Why, that Grinch even took the last can of Who-hash. Then he stuffed all the food up the chimney with glee, "And, now!", grinned the Grinch, "I will stuff up the tree."
Child: (pointing at the screen with curiosity)

Parent: And the Grinch grabbed the tree, and he started to shove, when he heard a small sound, like the coo of a dove. He turned around fast, and he saw a small Who! Little Cindy-Lou Who, who was not more than two. The Grinch caught this tiny Who daughter, who got out of bed for a cup of cold water. She stared at the Grinch and said, "Santy Claus, why? Why are you taking our Christmas tree? Why?"
Child: (listening intently, possibly a bit sleepy)

Parent: But you know that old Grinch was so smart and so slick, he thought up a lie, and he thought it up quick. "Why, my sweet little tot," the fake Santy Claus lied, "There's a light on this tree that won't light on one side, so I'm taking it home to my workshop, my dear, I'll fix it up there, then I'll bring it back here." And his fib fooled the child, then he patted her head, and he got a drink, and he sent her to bed. When Cindy-Lou Who went to bed with her cup, he went to the chimney and stuffed the tree up!
Child: (hugging the parent)
Parent: Okay, [inaudible 00:18:05]
Child: (sitting on parent's lap, looking at tablet)
Parent: Oh wait, he's taking it up the chimney.
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: Okay, can you push the button?
Child: What button?
Parent: (pointing at the corner of the tablet) At the corner.

Parent: (continuing to read from the tablet) Then the last thing he took was the log for their fire. Then he went up the chimney himself, the old liar. On their walls, he left nothing but hooks and some wire. And the one speck of food that he left in the house, was a crumb that was even too small for a mouse.
Child: (sitting still on parent's lap, looking at the tablet)
Parent: Then he did the same thing to the other Whos' houses.
Child: (sitting still on parent's lap, looking at the tablet)
Parent: He is one mean guy, go ahead.
Child: (sitting still on parent's lap, looking at the tablet, listening)

Parent: (continuing to read from the tablet) Leaving crumbs much too small for the other Whos' mouses. It was quarter past dawn, all the Whos still in bed, all the Whos still a-snooze, when he packed up his sled, packed it up with their presents, the ribbons, the wrappings, the tags, the tinsel, the trimmings, the trappings. Three thousand feet up the side of Mount Crumpit, he rode with his load to the tiptop to dump it. “Pooh-Pooh to the Whos!” He was Grinch-ish-ly humming, “They're finding out now that no Christmas is coming. They're just waking up. I know just what I'll do. Their mouths will hang open a minute or two. Then the Whos down in Who-ville will all cry?”
Child: (sitting still on parent's lap, listening)
Parent: (reading loudly) "BOO-HOO!"
Child: (sitting on parent's lap, looking down at the tablet)
Parent: "That's a noise," grinned the Grinch.
Child: (leans against parent, still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "He stared down at Who-ville, the Grinch popped his eyes, then he shook, what he saw..."
Child: (leans further back, slightly tilting back to look at the parent)
Parent: "And what happened then, well, in Who-ville they say, that the Grinch's small heart grew three sizes that day."
Child: (extends arms outward excitedly)
Parent: Like this big. [crosstalk 00:21:09]
Child: (leans back, looking down at the tablet)
Parent: "And the minute his heart didn't feel quite so tight, he whizzed with his load through the bright morning light."
Child: (looks at the parent, then reaches towards the tablet)
Parent: "Can you reach it?"
Child: (points at the tablet screen)
Parent: "And he,"
Child: (leans back, still pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "He himself,"
Child: (looks up suddenly)
Parent: "Wait, did we miss a page? Oh yeah."
Child: (leans back, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "And he, himself, the Grinch carved the roast beast."
Child: (looks at the parent)
Parent: "Oh, That's the end. Should we do one more short story? If you go to the arrow on the top left, there you go. It says short stories. These are the short stories."
